description: Backyard furnaces, communes and a famine killing tens of millions — Mao's deadliest economic experiment.
content_html:
From Recovery to Revolution

The early PRC years brought genuine economic recovery. The First Five-Year Plan (1953–57) was modelled closely on the Soviet system: heavy industry — steel, coal, machine tools — was the priority. With Soviet technical assistance, hundreds of large industrial projects were completed. Agricultural output grew steadily, partly through collectivisation, which was accelerated from 1955 as the Party absorbed individual peasant plots into cooperatives. By the end of the First Five-Year Plan, China had made genuine industrial gains. Then, in 1958, Mao abandoned the Soviet model entirely.

Key Fact

The Great Leap Forward, launched in 1958, aimed to transform China into a major industrial and agricultural power within fifteen years. Peasants were organised into people's communes of up to 10,000 households. Steel production targets were set that required even rural peasants to smelt metal in backyard furnaces, diverting labour from food production.

The People's Communes and Backyard Furnaces

By late 1958, approximately 26,000 communes had been established, absorbing virtually the entire rural population. Each commune was self-governing in theory but subject to CCP production targets in practice. Private plots were abolished. Meals were eaten in communal canteens. Peasants were told they were “eating from the same big pot.”

Steel production was an obsession. Mao set a target to overtake Britain in steel output within fifteen years. To meet local quotas, peasants were ordered to build backyard furnaces and smelt whatever metal they could find: farming tools, cooking pots, door hinges. The resulting iron was mostly too brittle to use. Meanwhile, the harvest of 1958 rotted in the fields because the agricultural labour force had been diverted to the steel campaign. Party officials who reported the true state of production were accused of pessimism and punished. This political dynamic — where honest reporting was dangerous — was central to why the disaster escalated.

Dazhai was a small commune in Shanxi Province, held up as a national model of socialist success. Its brigade leader, Chen Yonggui, was celebrated as a “model peasant” who had supposedly transformed barren hillside terraces into highly productive farmland through collective effort and political will. The slogan “In Agriculture, Learn from Dazhai” was promoted across China through the 1960s and 1970s. However, later investigations found that Dazhai’s reported yields had been systematically falsified and that the commune had received undisclosed state subsidies. Dazhai illustrates how the reporting system of the Great Leap Forward — where cadres faced punishment for honest accounts — generated systematically false data that concealed the scale of failure from the national leadership.

The Great Chinese Famine

Between 1959 and 1962, China experienced the deadliest peacetime famine in recorded history. Scholars have proposed widely differing estimates of the death toll: Frank Dikötter gives 45 million excess deaths; Yang Jisheng, a Chinese journalist whose own father died in the famine, estimates 36 million; Jasper Becker suggests 30 million; more conservative estimates from some Chinese researchers place the figure at 15–20 million. The range reflects genuine uncertainty in the historical data and the fact that Chinese government records were suppressed for decades. The Party’s own contemporary explanation — “three years of natural disaster” — was a deliberate misrepresentation: meteorological data shows that weather conditions in 1959–62 were not significantly worse than normal. The famine was overwhelmingly caused by policy failure.

Key Fact

Scholars estimate between 15 and 45 million deaths during the Great Leap Forward famine (1959–62). The CCP attributed the famine to “three years of natural disaster,” but later scholarship — including work by Frank Dikötter and Yang Jisheng — demonstrates the famine was primarily caused by policy failures, not weather.

In July 1959, at a leadership conference at Lushan, Defence Minister Peng Dehuai wrote Mao a private letter criticising the Great Leap Forward’s excesses. He noted food shortages, the uselessness of the backyard furnace steel, and the falsification of production figures. Mao chose to read the letter aloud to the conference delegates and accused Peng of leading a “military club” against the Party. Peng was stripped of his offices and subjected to criticism sessions. His purge sent an unmistakable signal: even the most senior officials who questioned Mao’s policies risked destruction. The result was that the Great Leap Forward continued for a further three years while the famine deepened.
exam_tip_html: When writing about the Great Leap Forward, avoid asserting a single death-toll figure as if it were established fact. Instead, use the range approach: “scholars estimate between 15 and 45 million deaths.” Naming at least one historian (Dikötter, Yang Jisheng) shows you understand that this is a contested field. For causation questions, aim to show how multiple factors (the commune system, reporting failures, the backyard furnace campaign, the Peng Dehuai purge) interacted — rather than simply listing them as separate items.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Great Leap Forward (1958) reorganised rural China into people’s communes and diverted agricultural labour into a failed steel campaign using backyard furnaces — causing a famine that killed an estimated 15–45 million people.
  • The CCP attributed the famine to “three years of natural disaster,” but scholars including Dikötter and Yang Jisheng demonstrate it was primarily a policy failure; honest reporting was suppressed after the purge of Peng Dehuai in 1959.
  • Dazhai commune was held up as a model of socialist success but its figures were falsified — a case study in how the Great Leap’s reporting system generated systematically false data that concealed the scale of failure.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the people's communes established during the Great Leap Forward.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A precise feature with specific supporting detail (e.g. size, abolition of private plots, communal eating). Secure: A relevant feature with basic supporting detail. Developing: A feature identified but without clear detail. Emerging: A vague or very limited statement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the First Five-Year Plan (1953–57).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct features with precise detail (e.g. Soviet model, heavy industry focus, Soviet technical assistance, output gains). Secure: Two features, each with some supporting detail. Developing: Two features but one or both lack evidence. Emerging: Only one feature or very limited information.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Great Leap Forward caused such a catastrophic famine.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more developed reasons linked together (e.g. agricultural labour diverted to steel, false reporting after Peng Dehuai's purge, commune system abolishing private incentives). Secure: Two reasons with supporting evidence. Developing: One well-developed reason or two thin points. Emerging: Simple statement with minimal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the purge of Peng Dehuai for the continuation of the Great Leap Forward.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated analysis of significance (immediate chilling effect on honest reporting, longer-term famine continuation, signals to future critics); counter-argument addressed. Secure: Clear argument about significance with evidence and some analysis. Developing: Relevant points with basic evidence; limited analysis. Emerging: Describes the purge with minimal argument about significance.

practice_questions.text: How far was the Great Leap Forward the main cause of the 1959–62 famine? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing multiple causes (policy failure, reporting system, purge of critics, weather as minor factor); specific evidence; considers whether other causes were more or less important. Secure: Clear argument with evidence from multiple causes; some weighing of relative importance. Developing: Mostly descriptive; limited weighing. Emerging: Simple narrative.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Dazhai commune was significant as a case study in the failure of the Great Leap Forward.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more developed reasons explaining both what Dazhai represented symbolically and what its later exposure revealed about systematic falsification. Secure: Two reasons with supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason or two undeveloped points. Emerging: Basic statement with little explanation.

glossary_terms.definition: China's first major economic development programme modelled on Soviet five-year plans, prioritising heavy industry.
The process by which private farms were merged into cooperatives and eventually people's communes under CCP direction.
Mao's 1958–62 programme to rapidly industrialise and collectivise China simultaneously, resulting in catastrophic famine.
Large collective units established during the Great Leap Forward, each containing thousands of families.
Small furnaces built by ordinary peasants during the Great Leap Forward to produce steel; the output was mostly too brittle to use.
China's Defence Minister who wrote to Mao in 1959 criticising the Great Leap Forward and was purged as a result.
